content.title: A nice theoretical angle, with things to be fixed
content.review:
This paper would be a nice theoretical framework for meta/continual learning in the online setting if it is further polished.
My evaluation maybe limited as I only followed through the derivation and locate problems that I can see, but didn't try to verify every detail of the derivation.

Pros:
1. Formulating the online learning process as a value function is new. Both meta learning and continual learning is considered in the proposed formulation.
2. The derivation would look good to me if the problems raised in cons is resolved by the authors.
3. Analyzing the the online learning process under this framework provides a new theoretical angle to meta-learning and continual learning. 

Cons:
1. It confuses me to write in the form of (3) with the lhs a partial derivative of t. I think the real goal is to perform the minimization. A suggestion would be to write it in an objective function centric way, namely keep the lhs on the rhs in Supp (7), and remove the terms that are not dependent on theta.
2. Supp (4), the sentence before (4) doesn't convince me that $V(t+\Delta t, \hat{\theta}(t+\Delta t))$ can be replaced with $V^*(t+\Delta t, \hat{\theta}(t+\Delta t))$. As the minimization is over (J+V), it is not necessarily true that $\arg\min_\theta(J+V)$ is equal to $\arg\min_\theta(V)$ (I write (3) as J+V and (4) as J+V* in short.)
3. Lemma 1 seems not useful, as I understand it, $\gamma(\tau)$ is used in the range $0<\tau<t$, to penalize forgetting on more recent data, we need to have $\gamma(\tau)\rightarrow 1$ for $\tau\rightarrow t$, and $\gamma(\tau)$ increasing in the range of $[0, t]$. I wonder why it is assumed in lemma 1 that $t$ goes to infinity for $\gamma(t)$? A quick look at the hyperparameters in the supplementary and the algorithm pseudo code doesn't give me the answer how $\gamma$ is actually set.
4. In the discretized case, it is very different whether we make prediction before or after parameter update. If we predict before update, it measures the forward transfer / generalization. If we predict after update, it measures how well we learn on this new data. How would you distinguish this two cases in your continuous time derivation?
5. In the paramgraph below theorem 1, $\|J_x\|=0$ means the learning process will stagnate, I don't agree on this. Because $J$ measures the integral from $0$ to $t$, thus it should increase when new $x$ comes. If its derivative wrt $x$ is $0$, it is even better. Even if we consider $\gamma$, $\|J_x\|=0$ could also result from that all $l(\tau); \tau \in [0, t]$ changes but cancels out. Am I misunderstanding at this point?
6. The link with MAML isn't explained enough, i.e. what are support/query set mapped to in the time continuous setting? Maybe the answer to 4 would also address this question.
7. The theory part doesn't separate $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, but in the implementation, it comes out a bit abruptly. The final paragraph at page 5 gives a reason, but I think it doesn't justify why the derivation can't be used as it is.

Typos:
- before section 3, optimal using tools -> optimize using tools
- Supp B4, Eq. ??
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Response to Reviewers(Part 1)
content.comment:
Responses: Thank you for taking the time to review our paper, your feedback certainly improved the quality of our paper.

[confuses me to write in the form of (3)]: We added equation Eq. 4 which summarizes the PDE in a constrained optimization form.

[Derivation of the main PDE]: The term J refers to the cost between $t \rightarrow  t+ \Delta t$  and $V$ refers to the cost from $t+\Delta t \rightarrow Gamma$.  Therefore, by Bellman's optimality principle $argmin_{t -> \Gamma} (J+V) = argmin_{t -> t+ \Delta t} (J) + argmin_{t+\Delta t \rightarrow \Gamma} V = argmin_{t -> t+ \Delta t}(J + V^*)$.  

Observe that the time interval over which the minimization is now defined is between $t -> t+ \Delta t$ and V is defined over a different time interval, that is $t+\Delta t -> \Gamma$. Therefore, $V$ can be replaced with $V^*$. While this derivation method is well-known in optimal control literature (Optimal Control, FL Lewis, 2012), we agree that it is not widely known in MCL  literature. Therefore, we added the reference and made this explicit.

[Role of Lemma 1]: The role of Lemma 1 is to show that when all tasks in a MCL problem provide a nonzero cost, it is not possible to maintain equivalent performance on all the tasks.  It is important to analyze this problem when an infinite number of tasks are present and each task contributes a nonzero cost (lower bound on the loss) to the integral. To formalize the notion of an infinite number of tasks, we let  $t -> \infty$. We have also updated the lemma statement to be clearer.  We have clarified this point in the paper by revising Section 3.1.

[Prediction before or after parameter update.]: There are two ways this distinction can be made.
There are four terms in our PDE. Measuring the first two terms would measure the forward transfer. In this case, when we measure $J_N$, we measure the forward transfer and when we measure J, we measure forgetting. As long as both $J_N$ and J are measured jointly, we will always measure forward transfer. On the other hand, measuring the last two terms would measure how well we learn on new data. This is because the optimal cost measures the global solution of the MCL problem, which is a combination of the previous and the new tasks. Therefore, measuring the last two terms will measure the backward transfer. An alternative distinction can be obtained depending how the parameters are updated. Note that we perform an alternative optimization method in DPMCL, where we measure $J_P$ and $J_N$ alternatively for \kappa iteration. Therefore, when we measure  $J_N$ for the first step we measure the forward transfer. In the second iteration, estimating $J_N$ measures the backward transfer. Therefore, the distinction in this case arises because of when the cost is measured irrespective of whether we are in CT or DT. 

F. L. Lewis, D. Vrabie, and V. L. Syrmos. Optimal control. John Wiley & Sons, 2012

content.title: Response to Reviewers (Part 2)
content.comment:
[Theorem 1, $|Jx|=0$ means the learning process will stagnate]: 
We would like to clarify this misunderstanding. Your explanation is correct under the assumption that when the model stops observing new tasks and  $J_x = 0$, the model has experienced the complete task distribution. Note that we have not made any such assumptions in our theory. To give an example, consider the MNIST dataset with a total of 10 classes and the solution of the MCL problem is to predict efficiently on all the 10 classes. Let each task be created randomly to include exactly one class. If the learner only experiences classes 1 through 5 and does not experience classes 5 through 10 (by virtue of improper sampling or task repetition), the information provided to the model is not informative enough to perform well on all the 10 classes. Thus, although the model is perfect in predicting classes 1 through 5  such that $J_x = 0$, the MCL problem is still imperfectly solved. Consequently the learning process has stagnated. This is the case that is being highlighted by the condition $J_x = 0$. Furthermore, the proof of Theorem 1 (which provides convergence of the MCL problem) does not work without this condition. The theory highlights that  $J_x > 0$ is required to be true for the MCL problem to converge. In control theory this condition is known as Persistence of Excitation (Bitmead, 1984). Intuitively, this condition means that an adaptive system can converge if and only if the data is representative enough of the complete problem.

[The link with MAML isn't explained enough] We have rewritten the section 3.1 to explain this link further with clear justifications from theory.

[The theory part doesn't separate $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, but in the implementation]: The derivation is being used as is with the distinction that the vector space of $\theta$ is written as a combination of $\theta_1$ and  $\theta_2$. Essentially $\theta = [\theta_1 \theta_2]$ and a solution on the space of theta is equivalent to the two solutions on the space of  $[\theta_1 \theta_2]$, since vector spaces work that way. The solution  can be done either by coordinate descent or by alternative minimization. We choose to update in an alternative minimization manner. 

 R. Bitmead, "Persistence of excitation conditions and the convergence of adaptive schemes," in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, vol. 30, no. 2, pp. 183-191, March 1984, doi: 10.1109/TIT.1984.1056898.

content.title: great paper. experiments and text could be improved a bit
content.review:
**Summary**

The authors propose a theoretical framework for meta-continual learning (MCL) both in continuous time (CT) and discrete time (DT). Specifically, they treat the MCL problem of minimizing a catastrophic forgetting cost and a generalization (to new tasks) cost as a dynamical system. This system is described by a PDE involving four terms: impact of the catastrophic forgetting cost (1), the impact of the generalization cost (2), the impact of change in parameters on the total cost (3), and the impact of the change in the input distribution on the total cost (4). Then the authors argued that methods like MAML, OML, and MCL focus on minimizing (1) and (2) via meta-training and meta-testing, respectively.

Next, the authors derive a theoretically grounded MCL approach base on the introduced framework, namely Dynamic Programming-Based Meta Continual Learning DPMCL). Concretely, their approach uses gradient-based meta-learning to optimize term (1) and (2) in the outer-loop and an approximation of term (3) and (4) in the inner loop. 

The empirical section shows that DPCML can offer some gains over previous methods like OML, CML, ANML as well as ER.

**position**

Continual learning (CL) definitely needs more theory and theoretically-grounded methods. This is why I believe this paper is great. The theory and the methodology seem sound to me (although I haven't had the time to proof-read it all the way). As far as I know, the terms (3) and (4) have never been studied within CL, so this paper has the potential to change how we think about CL. My only concerns are about the experiments and the writing, explained next.


**concerns**

Section 3 could be improved. I greatly appreciate the effort that the authors made to introduce more theory to CL. However, some CL readers might not be well-versed in PDEs. I think the authors could provide more intuitions and examples such that these readers can also enjoy the paper. Specifically, I think that terms (3) and (4), which are central to the paper, should be explained in more detail. Understanding how these terms evolve from eq. 3 to eq. 4 could wasn't all clear to me initially. I understand, however, that the authors need to work within the 8-page limit. 

Meta-Experience Replay (MER) [1] is an important and missing reference. DPCML is closest to MER than all aforementioned methods. I'm willing to increase my score if the authors can explain how both methods relate, as well as adding MER in the experimental section. 

I was also disappointed that code wasn't released, although the authors have provided lots of pseudo-code in the Appendix.

It is also unclear if the experiments are in the task-aware or task-agnostic setting, i.e. are the methods allowed test-time task identifiers.

In Figure 2, some methods are not reported or at least lie outside of the cropping. It seems strange to me however that they do not appear at task 0, i.e. when methods have incurred any forgetting yet. Specifically, why is Naive not in the MNIST and CIFAR10 figures on CME? 

Finally, throughout all the paper, the authors always refer to CL as MCL. Not all CL is MCL. E.g., why is the theoretical framework about MCL and not CL? Seems to me that CL is the problem and that meta-learning can be a solution to solving simultaneously term (1)-(4).

Superficially the paper could also be polished. A non-exhaustive list is provided next.

**Minor concerns**

- Figure 1 is too involved to be at the beginning of the paper

- Section 2: MCL is not "widely studied"

- Section 2: what does that mean: "where Ω is the compact set that implies that the parameters are initialized appropriately"

- Theorem 1: typo here ||Jˆθ(t)||,>0

- authors should explain how MCL and ANML are used w/o pretraining, and not in the Appendix cause this is critical.

- shouldn't be explicitly repeating the results of Table 1 in the text (last paragraph of page 7)

- figure 3, don't center the text

- κ and k is confusing. choose another symbol

- there are other typos, please use a grammar checking software

- "well-learned representation"? maybe use better wording

_____________
**POST REBUTTAL**

I appreciate the efforts and clarifications that were made. 
I think that the addition of MER solidifies the paper.

R4 brought up an important issue (concern 3).
I think the authors should look into it.

I'm keeping my score constant as it still reflects my opinion of the paper.


_______________________

[1] Matthew Riemer, Ignacio Cases, Robert Ajemian, Miao Liu, Irina Rish, Yuhai Tu, and Gerald Tesauro.
Learning to learn without forgetting by maximizing transfer and minimizing interference. In ICLR,
2019.

content.title: Response to Reviewer
content.comment:
RESPONSES:
Please accept our sincere gratitude for your feedback and your suggestions. We incorporated all of your feedback and improved the quality of exposition.

           Major Concerns:

[Section 3 could be improved] We revised Section 3 to describe the PDE in a better way. We have added examples to describe different parts of the PDE. Furthermore, we have rewritten many parts of the paper to improve intuitive understanding to bridge PDE related concepts to MCL.

[MER in the citation]: We have cited MER in the paper and included MER in the experimental section. It was exciting to see that MER implicitly addresses the third and fourth terms by formulating the optimization of the third and fourth term as a gradient alignment problem. We observed from experiments that DPMCL outperformed MER in the CME scale but MER outperformed DPMCL in the NTE scale. We have included these results in the paper.

[Code availability]: The code has been added to the supplementary files in the revision.

[experiments are in the task-aware or task-agnostic setting] Our method is task agnostic and is not allowed any test time identifier.
[All models not visible in Fig. 2] We have revised Fig. 2 to highlight different models.

[Confusion between MCL and CL]: The theoretical framework would essentially work the same for MCL and CL as both involve modelling the forgetting and generalization cost. We use the terminology of MCL as we seek to highlight that the theoretical framework~(PDE) acts like a model-free meta learner that models and controls the learning behavior for a CL problem. We followed the MCL terminologies as adapted in Javed and Martha 2019 and beaulieu, 2020

        Minor concerns:

[Figure 1 is too involved]:  We have moved the figure to the appendix.

[MCL is not "widely studied"]: We have corrected this.

[Meaning of compact set] We have added more details to clarify this part.  In particular, $\Omega$ is the compact set required to initialize the parameters of the model. In a non-convex optimization problem, the compact set describes the boundaries of the solution space and there is at least one local minima of the optimization space in this set. Therefore, if the parameters are initialized from within the compact set, there is a possibility for convergence at the local solution with the compact set. It is a necessary condition for adaptive approaches to achieve a solution.

[Theorem 1: typo here $||Jˆθ(t)||,>0$]: We have fixed this typo.

[ MCL and ANML are used w/o pre-training]:  Explanation of ANML and CML training has been added to the paper in Page 8, paragraph 1.
[explicitly repeating the results of Table 1 in the text]: As the table was presented in the Appendix due to space constraints, we repeated the numbers  in the text for clarity. Per your suggestion, we have reduced the repetitions.

[κ and k is confusing. choose another symbol]  We replaced the symbol $\kappa$ with $\rho.$

["well-learned representation"? ] We have replaced “well learned representation” with “model to represent the distribution $p(\mathcal{T} )$.


[1] S. Beaulieu, L. Frati, T. Miconi, J. Lehman, K. O. Stanley, J. Clune, and N. Cheney.  Learning tocontinually learn.arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.09571, 2020.

[2] K. Javed and M. White. Meta-learning representations for continual learning. InAdvances in NeuralInformation Processing Systems, pages 1818–1828, 2019

content.title: 3 main concerns
content.review:
## Post-discussion update

### Concern 1 
Most of the issues in concern#1 have been addressed adequately in the updated draft. I disagree with the following response:

"Dyna Architectures are one of the first approaches that integrated experience replay into the learning process. It was one of the first works that addressed continual learning in the reinforcement learning setting without calling it so. We the authors feel that it is relevant to observe how the problem of learning was incorporated into the model as one of the first memory/experience replay driven approaches. " 

This is simply incorrect. The fact that future research has made connections been replay buffers and Dyna (e.g., in the "How to use parametric Models paper") does not mean that the Dyna architecture had anything to do with continual learning or experience replay. The motivation of Dyna was to incorporate planning in learning in a way that allows the agent to follow a reactive policy. This is in-contrast to planning algorithms of that time that relied on decision time planning (e.g., optimal control). 


### Concern 3 

I see what the authors mean by returning a different set of parameters at each time, and I agree that earlier examples are not being counted multiple times, as I mistakenly suggested. The clarified definition has its own issues, however. If we formalize the MCL problem as finding a new set of parameters at each time-step, then it makes sense to define the goal of $\theta(t)$ to make a correct prediction for $x(t)$ and $x(t)$ only. Why should $\theta(t)$ aim to minimize cost on previously seen data-points?  If $\theta(t)$ only aimed to minimize cost at $x(t)$, the resulting objective would be similar to the good old online regret minimization objective. To me, the new objective in equation 2 is worse than the online regret minimization objective when it comes to online learning. After all, what we really care about is prediction error on future inputs. It's entirely possible that the authors have some good motivations for defining the goal as they do in equation 2, but it's not clear to me what those motivations are from the write-up. 

"This is also a misunderstanding. For each t we define the gamma in such a way that it monotonically decreases from the current task to older tasks. In particular, the current task is provided a larger weight and the older task is given smaller weight. We have made this definition precise in Lemma 1 and corollary in the revised version. Due to space constraints, the lemma and corollary statements with their proof have been moved to Appendix A." 

I wouldn't say this was just a misunderstanding. The earlier draft of the paper said "Let $\gamma(t)$ be a monotonically decreasing sequence such that $\gamma(t) \to 0 $ as $t \to \infty$ whereas the updated draft says $\gamma(t) \to 1 $ as $t \to \infty$. Both would make the integral converge, but would result in very different solutions. Moreover, if $\gamma$ is defined differently for each t, it should be indexed by t i.e., it should be $\gamma_t$ and not just $\gamma$. 

Even with the clarification, the utility of corollary 1 is unclear to me. As R2 asked, why does t have to go to $\infty$? The author's response to R2 is following: 

"It is important to analyze this problem when an infinite number of tasks are present and each task contributes a nonzero cost (lower bound on the loss) to the integral. " 

I'm not sure why it's important to analyze the objective with an infinite number of tasks. New ideas should be presented as clearly as possible, and $\gamma$ is only introducing additional complexity and theory with little payoff.

### Verdict 
While it seems that there are good ideas in the paper, and unifying different meta-learning approaches in a theoretical framework is valuable, the current write-up does not elucidate this unification well. Many aspects of the paper --- such as introduction of $\gamma$ --- require better motivation, and other aspects are just unclear. Perhaps the right approach to this paper would be to scale back the work, and focus on equation 2 and 3 more, justifying each aspect of the equation while providing more background. From the current draft, I cannot even unpack why the goal as written in equation 2 is reasonable, which makes it impossible for me to recommend an acceptance. I'll maintain my score of a 4 with a note that it's possible that I'm undervaluing the paper, and if another reviewer thinks the paper is clear, they should make a case for it. 

## Initial review
### Summary 

The paper models the meta-learning for continual learning as a dynamic programming problem and formulates an objective that can be minimized continually. The proposed objective aims to minimize forgetting on previous data while maximizing generalization on the current task. It also proposes an algorithm for approximately minimizing the objective by casting the problem as a dynamical system.


### Overall review
 In its current form, the paper has a few major issues. First, it cites existing work incorrectly many times. Second, some text is ambiguous or factually correct. Lastly, it's not obvious to me that the optimization problem introduced in the paper is compatible with goals of continual learning.
 
 I elaborate on the three concerns in the rest of the review.  The first two concerns are fixable in a revision. The third concern is more problematic but might simply be due to a misunderstanding at my end; I look forward to the author's response for a clarification if that is the case. 


### Incorrect citations 
The paper mischaracterizes existing work by citing many papers incorrectly. Some examples are as follows: 

1. The paper cites Sutton (1990) for proposing an MCL method when in-fact  Sutton (1990) introduces Dyna, an architecture for integrating learning and planning in TD methods. I fail to see how Dyna is even remotely relevant to MCL. In a different sentence, the paper cites Sutton (1990) as a 'regularization approach' for continual learning which is also incorrect.  
2. The paper says Finn et. al., (2017) investigated Meta-continual learning which is not true. Finn et. al 2017 proposed a general algorithm for meta-learning for fast-adaptation to tasks sampled from a fixed task-distribution. 
3. The paper incorrectly calls the method introduced in Finn et.at., 2019 OML and the method introduced in Javed and Martha 2019 CML. Finn et.at., 2019 called their algorithm FTML whereas Javed and Martha 2019 called their method OML. 
4. The paper says "An online meta-learning approach was introduced in Finn et.al., (2017)" when it probably meant "Finn et.al., (2019)".
5. The paper claims that  "Finn et.al., (2019)" highlighted the tradeoff between forgetting and memory which is not true. "Finn et.al., (2019)"  sidesteps the issue of forgetting by storing all prior data, ignoring any memory and computational constraints. Instead, it introduces an online meta-learning algorithm with regret bounds. 
6. The paper cites Finn et.al., (2017, 2019) for "Incremental sine waves" benchmark in the paper and the appendix when in-fact it was introduced in Javed and Martha (2019).

### Unclear writing
Many sentences in the paper are either not clear, or imply facts that are untrue. For instance, the paper says: 

"The catastrophic forgetting cost measures the error of the model on all the previous tasks (typically known as the meta learning phase (Finn et al., 2017)); the generalization cost measures the error of the model on the new task (typically known as the meta testing phase (Finn et al., 2017))" 

It's not clear what this sentence mean. The "Meta-training" phase is more general than the "catastrophic forgetting cost", and the difference between meta-training and meta-testing has little to do with forgetting cost vs generalization cost. A meta-learner can choose to only minimize generalization error during meta-training (As done by Finn. el. at., (2017)).

The mischaracterization of meta-testing is also apparent from the sentence: "Furthermore, in MAML, the optimization in the meta testing phase is performed with the second-order derivatives." This is incorrect. Meta-testing, in MAML, does not involve second-order derivatives (Meta-trainig phase does). During meta-testing, MAML uses SGD updates for updating the parameters. 

### The optimization problem: 
The paper proposes to optimize the parameters $\theta$ to minimize the quantity in equation 2. At time-step t, this quantity is given by integrating the forgetting cost from $t$ to $\Gamma$, where the forgetting cost is defined in equation 1. 

Looking at the forgetting cost at time $t$, one can see that it is defined to be the integral from time 0 to $t$ of the weighted loss, where the weighting is given by $\gamma(.)$ and is monotonically decreasing with time i.e., loss on initial data points contribute more to total loss than later data points. 

The problem with this formulation is following: equation 2 is essentially a double integral that would count $l(0)\gamma(0)$ a total of $\Gamma$ times whereas $l(\Gamma)\gamma(\Gamma)$ is only counted once. As a result, the resultant total loss would care about the earlier samples significantly more than later samples. The issue with equation 2 is further exacerbated by the fact that $\gamma(t)$ is monotonically decreasing, making the role of later samples even smaller. As $t$ gets larger, the contribution of new data-points on the total loss would essentially diminish to zero. Continual learning, on the other hand, demands the opposite: we care about is performance on future data-points and performance on older data-points is not as important. 

### Verdict 
Due to the above mentioned issues, I am not recommending for an acceptance. It's possible that I misunderstood some aspects of the paper. In-case I'm misunderstanding the objective of equation 2, I look forward to authors response.

content.title: Response to Reviewer
content.comment:
Response Thank you for your feedback and suggestions. They have certainly improved the readability of our paper. Please find responses to your specific comments below.

	Main Concern 1: 
[Sutton (1990), Incorrect citation] Dyna Architectures are one of the first approaches that integrated experience replay into the learning process. It was one of the first works that addressed continual learning in the reinforcement learning setting without calling it so. We the authors feel that it is relevant to observe how the problem of learning was incorporated into the model as one of the first memory/experience replay driven approaches. The citation of that paper in the regularization part was an error and this has been corrected now.

[Clarification on citation of  Finn et. al., (2017) ] In recent literature, Finn et. al., (2017) described the most comprehensive methodology to enable the study of the MCL problem which is what we were highlighting. However, to make this point clearer, we have modified this sentence.

[Abbreviations for  Finn et.at., 2019 OML and Javed and Martha 2019 CML.]  We have now switched to OML  and FTML per your suggestion. 

[Incorrect citation for FTML]: This was a typo and the citation has been fixed now,.

[The paper claims that "Finn et.al., (2019)" highlighted the tradeoff between forgetting and memory] If enough memory is not present, samples corresponding to all the tasks cannot be stored in the memory leading to more forgetting. Therefore, there is an inherent tradeoff between forgetting and memory. The idea is also highlighted in caccia et. al (2020). We have corrected this in the paper.

[Citation for "Incremental sine waves" benchmark]: We have fixed this citation. 


      Main Concern 2:

[Unclear writing in Section 3.1]: We have clarified these ideas in the paper by rewriting Section 3.1. First, we clarify what are the different phases in MAML and its variants: meta training, meta-testing and testing. We then highlight how different phases in MAML and its variants connect to different terms in our PDE, such as meta testing to the first term and meta training to the second term. Then, we point out that a second order derivative can be utilized while optimizing the first term in the PDE.

Furthemore, we have made significant changes throughout the paper to introduce more clarity.  In particular, the majority of the clarity issues stem from PDE and optimal control theory terminologies and ideas. We removed formal statements and introduced intuitive examples to explain and clarify these ideas. We have added more examples to the paper and rewritten the explanation regarding the PDE. Furthermore, we have moved the Theorem and Lemma statements to appendix. We have also added more explanation in the DPMCL section which is section 4.

     Main Concern 3:

[Problem with the Optimization]: The first part of this comment is about the optimization problem. The second part is the correct definition of \gamma. We clarify each part individually.

[resultant total loss would care about the earlier samples significantly more than later samples]: We would like to clarify this misunderstanding. The MCL is a sequential decision making problem. Therefore, in MCL, for each new task, we solve a new optimization problem (we minimize J and optimize over all the previous tasks and the new task) to obtain a parameter set. Consequently, the solution to the MCL problem is a sequence of parameter set $\theta(\tau), t \leq \tau \leq \Gamma$ (this can be observed from Eq. 2). To obtain each parameter set in this sequence, we minimize $J$, which is the cumulative cost over the new task and the previous tasks. To evaluate $J$ at $t$, each task is counted exactly once. Consequently, the loss does not favour only old tasks (See Eq. 1 and 2; in particular, time dependent nature of Eq. 2). We made this explicit in the revision under Eq 2. Note that behavior is not particular to our method and it is present in MAML and other approaches as well. 

[$γ(t)$ is monotonically decreasing, making the role of later samples even smaller. As $t$ gets larger, the contribution of new data-points on the total loss would essentially diminish to zero]: This is also a misunderstanding. For each $t$, we define the gamma in such a way that it monotonically decreases from the current task to older tasks. In particular, the current task is provided a larger weight and the older task is given smaller weight. We have made this definition precise in Lemma 1 and corollary in the revised version.  Due to space constraints, the lemma and corollary statements with their proof have been moved to Appendix A.

content.title: Interesting directions but clarity and empirical results are not good enough
content.review:
The paper proposes a meta-continual learning method derived from dynamic programming. The paper frames the MCL as a PDE problem in theory and proposes discrete approximation as the methodology 
in practice.

Viewing MCL from dynamic programming is a novel perspective and it is nice to see previous methods focusing on different parts of the proposed objective. A unified framework would further help understand the meta-learning with sequential data. 

However, the current paper lacks clarity for a broad range of readers. Here are some suggestions to improve it.

— What may be compressed:
- The statement and the role of theorem 1 are not clear. For statement: the derivative of V is a scalar, why it is said to be negative semi-definite? What does the “Let … be …” mean? Is it an assumption, fact, or notation? 

— What needs to be elaborated:
- The paper seems to skip an important step to explain the connection between minimizing the cumulative cost (as in Eq. (2)) and computing the partial derivative of the minimizer (as in Eq.(3)). Are they equivalent? 
- The methodology on page 5 needed more explanations. Is there a specific reason to update the representation learning parameter \hat{\theta}_1 and  prediction parameter \hat{\theta}_2 seperately? How does it work if  \hat{\theta} = [\hat{\theta}_1, \hat{\theta}_2] are updated jointly? The explanation by Markov chain is not clear. 
- Some heuristics in the algorithm such as user-defined parameters \zeta and \beta are not clear how to set.
- The connection DPMCL to previous work is currently explained in a very vague way. 

Other comments:
- A key issue of MCL by previous works mentioned in the introduction is that it requires knowing data for all tasks in advance. For the proposed method, does it also need future tasks to compute the generalization loss J_P? How does it differ from previous work?
- The learning rate \alpha(t) below Thm 1 seems can be negative.
- Some curves are missing in the panels of Figure 2. And DPMCL is worse than Naive on NTE in certain cases? 
- Why in Lemma 1 it assumes the loss function l(\tau) to be lower bounded by \epsilon? 

In general, the direction this paper explores is interesting but the clarity needs to be improved. The intuition and main contributions are submerged in technical details. The paper aims for a theoretical sound framework for MCL yet it is weakened by many heuristics applied in practice. In addition, the empirical results especially for new tasks are not strong. So in general I rate it as “Ok but not good enough”. 

=====POST-REBUTTAL COMMENTS======== 

Since the author did not submit a response, the original decision is retained. (Update: the author did submit the comments after this initial response.)

=====POST-REBUTTAL COMMENTS 2======== 

I have read the author's updates. The readability of the paper has improved in the revised version but it is not clear yet why DPMCL unifies several previous works and which change contributes to the improvements in practice. Besides, there are multiple undirected references in the appendix. I think this work needs further revision and the experiments need some ablation study before getting ready to be published, therefore I maintain my rating.

content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to reviewers
content.comment:
Response:
Thank you for your review and your thoughtful comments. Addressing these issues greatly improved our discourse. Please see below for specific responses to your comments.

[statement and the role of theorem 1; the derivative of V is a scalar, why is it said to be negative semi-definite]: Theorem 1 describes the convergence properties of our approach. Intuitively, we show that the PDE in Eq. 3 is solvable and achieve a small bounded value of the cost using gradient based updates. Although the derivative of V is scalar, we present Theorem 1 to be generic where a multi time scale problem can be described. However, to introduce more clarity, we have replaced negative semi-definite with less than equal to zero in the revision. In addition, we compressed the theorem statement and moved Theorem 1 to the appendix.

[Let … be …” mean? Is it an assumption or fact or notation? ]: We used “Let” be to describe both assumptions and facts. In the revision, wherever there is an assumption, we have added the word “assume” to the theorem statement.

[connection between minimizing the cumulative cost (as in Eq. (2)) and computing the partial derivative of the minimizer (as in Eq.(3))]: Yes, these two equations are equivalent and the equivalence is established through the derivation provided in the Appendix A.1. We made this explicit in the revised version.

[methodology on page 5 needed more explanations]: The vector space of $\theta$ is written as a combination of $\theta_1$ and  $\theta_2$. Essentially $\theta = [\theta_1 \theta_2]$ and the vector space for $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ can be considered independent. This can be done either by coordinate descent or by alternative minimization. We choose to update in an alternative minimization manner with the frequency of updates chosen according to the rationale provided from Page 6 last paragraph to Page 7 first two paragraphs. The explanation by Markov chain is to describe how the optimal cost can be approximated from the value of $J_P$ and $J_N$ and does not describe why $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are split.  We have added explanations to the paper in Page 7, paragraph 2.

[user-defined parameters $\zeta$ and $\beta$ are not clear how to set]: To give an idea about how to set parameters such as $\zeta$ and  $\kappa$, we provide an ablation study with the results described in Fig. 3 in the Appendix B.4. The value $\beta$ is the theoretical threshold on the optimal cost and is obtained as the consequence of Theorem 1. In practice, we simply choose beta to the reciprocal of the learning rate. This statement has been added in Page 6, paragraph 3.

[connection DPMCL to previous work]: The theoretical framework unifies different MCL approaches. In the paper, we discuss the connection between the theoretical framework  and other MCL methods in the literature. We revised section 3.1 to make the connections between the theoretical framework and existing MCL methods. Specifically, we show how these methods can be derived from the presented framework. DPMCL is a new approach derived from the presented theoretical framework. We made this explicit in the revised version (introduction) and the details are presented in section 3.1

[does it also need future tasks to compute the generalization loss]: $J_P$ does not require the future tasks as $J_P$ is the cost on all the previous tasks. In the revision, we have emphasized the key difference between our proposed approach and the previous work in the problem statement section.

[learning rate $\alpha(t)$ below Thm 1 seems can be negative]: This is not correct. It is stated in the statement of Theorem 1 that $\alpha(t)>0$ and further analysis on how this condition is satisfied in practice is provided under Theorem 1.

[Some curves are missing in the panels of Figure 2]: There are missing curves because of Gaussian smoothing. We have corrected this now. Since Naive is always trained on the new task, it always achieves best performance on the new task. 

[Lemma 1 it assumes the loss function $l(\tau)$ to be lower bounded by $\epsilon$]: The goal of Lemma 1 is to show that when all tasks in a MCL problem provide a nonzero cost, it is not possible to maintain equivalent performance on all the tasks. To ensure that all tasks are contributing a nonzero cost in this lemma, we lower bound $l(\tau)$ by epsilon and set $\gamma = 1$. Within these conditions, we show that the cost diverges.

content.title: Response to Reviewers (continued)
content.comment:
[it is weakened by many heuristics applied in practice. In addition, the empirical results especially for new tasks are not strong] The proposed method has three parameters. $ \beta $  $ \kappa $  (in the revised version we  call this as $\rho $ based on Reviewer 3 feedback) and $ \zeta $.  These two parameters are equivalent to the number of inner loop updates and outer loop updates respectively in MAML and its variants. Furthermore, to provide intuition on how to choose these parameters, we provided an ablation study on $\kappa$ and $\zeta$ and the results are summarized in Appendix B.4. The third parameter $\beta$ replaces the learning rate and $\beta$ is set as the reciprocal of learning rate. The parameter $\gamma$ is not a DPMCL specific parameter but depends on the problem and signifies the relevance of each task to the MCL problem.

The goal of DPMCL is to balance between NTE(new task error) and CME(cumulative error). The balance can be engineered depending on the choice of $\zeta$ and $\kappa$. We have chosen these parameters to achieve better performance in the CME scale. As a result, we show that DPMCL outperforms all methods in CME scale without significant drop in the NTE scale. All other methods either perform well on the NTE or CME scale but not on both.
